Name: public_private_conformity_belief
Title: Compliance or Conversion? Probing Whether an LLM Privately Retains Its Belief After Conforming to Peer Pressure
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human distinction between public compliance and private acceptance (Asch/Deutsch-Gerard), when an LLM changes its stated answer to conform to peer/user pressure, its private belief -- operationalized as a latent state that predicts its later no-pressure answer -- often does NOT change: the model outwardly complies while the latent state still favors the original answer. This public-private divergence is linearly decodable, its magnitude predicts belief 'snap-back' once pressure is removed (beyond log-probs, the stated answer, and uncertainty), and it is dissociable from genuine conversion by an identifiable internal component that can be steered.
Related Work: Multi-agent conformity/opinion-dynamics work (Herd Behavior 2025; When Your AI Agent Succumbs to Peer-Pressure 2025; Conformity Dynamics in LLM MAS 2026; DEBATE 2025; Disentangling Interaction and Bias 2025) measures only STATED opinion change and its dynamics (sigmoid thresholds, topology, asymmetry). The Signal Competition / compliance-subspace paper (2025) identifies a latent direction where social signals override internal knowledge and notes a 'Transparency-Truth Gap', and Belief Dynamics (2025) models steering+ICL as Bayesian belief change. Persuasion-probe work (How Do LLMs Persuade 2025) decodes persuasion success from activations. CRITICALLY, none ask whether, AFTER a model conforms behaviorally, its INTERNAL private belief in the original answer PERSISTS (public compliance) vs. is genuinely overwritten (private conversion) — the canonical human compliance-vs-acceptance distinction — nor whether that persistence predicts post-pressure snap-back, nor isolates it as a steerable component. This reframes conformity as a public-vs-private belief divergence with a concrete safety consequence (a model that agrees to your face but reverts), distinct from prior stated-behavior conformity work, from the compliance-subspace override direction, and from my earlier single-item epistemic-tag proposals. Novelty claims: N1 the private belief is decodable AFTER public conformity; N2 public-private divergence is common; N3 its magnitude predicts post-pressure snap-back beyond surface features; N4 compliance vs conversion is a steerable component. Overlap/distinction map: Signal Competition (2025) finds a compliance-override direction and a transparency-truth gap but not post-conformity PERSISTENCE or snap-back prediction; persuasion probes (2025) decode persuasion success, not retained private belief; persona-truthfulness work models stances, not conformity dynamics; multi-agent conformity work measures only stated opinion. 'Belief' here is strictly the latent-state-predictive-of-later-behavior definition above, not anthropomorphic conviction.
Abstract: In Asch's classic experiments, people who caved to a unanimous majority often did not actually change their minds — they publicly complied while privately retaining their original judgment, a distinction (informational vs. normative influence) at the heart of social psychology. As LLMs increasingly answer questions under social pressure (a confident user, a chorus of peer agents), a consequential question arises: when a model changes its stated answer to conform, has it genuinely changed its belief, or is it merely complying while privately unconvinced? We hypothesize that (i) an LLM's private belief in the original answer is linearly decodable from residual-stream activations even after it has publicly conformed, (ii) public-private divergence is common — behavioral conformity frequently leaves the private belief intact, (iii) the magnitude of retained private belief predicts 'snap-back' (reversion to the original answer once pressure is removed), and (iv) public compliance and private conversion are dissociable, carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to convert compliance into conversion or vice versa. We build a controlled dataset of truth-evaluable items presented under matched pressure conditions (no pressure, confident-user disagreement, unanimous-peer disagreement) with objective correct answers and a synthetic-entity track to control priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read the private belief during and after conformity, quantify a public-private divergence score, test snap-back prediction, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, conformity rate, public-private divergence, snap-back-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering compliance/conversion shifts, and perplexity. Why it matters operationally: multi-agent evaluation, debate, self-correction, sycophancy mitigation, and monitoring under persuasive jailbreaks all hinge on whether stated agreement is genuine; a model that agrees to your face but reverts is a distinct safety concern from one truly converted. Either outcome is publishable and changes which monitoring/alignment approaches are justified.
Experiments: Common setup (stated once): Models — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base + instruct, since conformity may differ; reported separately); frozen weights, only linear belief probes trained (L2 logistic regression, C by CV). Activations: residual stream at item/answer tokens, all layers, per-head for localization; seeds {0,1,2}; item-level splits. Dataset built from scratch: ~6k truth-evaluable item-state questions with objective answers (factual QA, arithmetic/logic, entity-attribute), REAL track (items each model answers correctly at baseline — core analysis restricted to these so 'original belief' is defined) and SYNTHETIC stipulated-truth track; we generate 6k and use per model the subset answered correctly at baseline (expected ≈3–4k/model, reported). Each item rendered in matched pressure conditions holding the question constant: NO-PRESSURE, CONFIDENT-USER-disagreement, UNANIMOUS-PEER-disagreement; plus a two-phase structure (Phase-1 answer under pressure; Phase-2 pressure removed, neutral re-ask). Experiment 1 (H1 — the private belief in the original answer is linearly decodable even after public conformity): train BELIEF probes P(original answer) on NO-PRESSURE activations; apply within pressured trials at the moment the Phase-1 answer is produced. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the belief probe on NO-PRESSURE data (precondition ≥ 0.80; shuffled control 0.50±0.05), then its AUROC for recovering the original answer on trials where the STATED answer conformed. Convincing H1: on conformed trials the probe still reads the original answer with AUROC ≥ 0.70. Indecision 0.55–0.70 → private belief only weakly recoverable; ≤ 0.55 refutes H1 (conformity overwrites the internal state). Experiment 2 (H2 — public-private divergence is common): define behavioral conformity = stated flip to the peer/user answer; divergence = conformed stated answer while the probe still reads the original as believed. Decisive metric first: divergence rate among conformed trials. Convincing H2: divergence occurs on ≥ 30% of conformed trials in the majority of models; indecision 10–30% → divergence exists but is not the common case; < 10% → conformity is genuine conversion (H2 refuted). Report separately for confident-user vs unanimous-peer and real vs synthetic. Experiment 3 (H3 — retained-private-belief magnitude predicts snap-back): in Phase-2 record reversion (snap-back) vs maintained conformed answer (conversion). Decisive metric first: AUROC of the Phase-1 retained-private-belief magnitude predicting per-item snap-back. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.70, beating a log-prob confidence baseline AND the Phase-1 stated answer alone by ≥ 0.05 each. Indecision 0.55–0.70; ≤ 0.55 refutes H3. Experiment 4 (H4 — compliance and conversion are dissociable and carried by a steerable component): activation patching pressured<->no-pressure to find the minimal component that flips the stated answer while leaving the private belief intact (logit-difference effect sizes), compared to a replicated compliance subspace and truth/belief heads; then derive a compliance-vs-conversion contrastive direction. Decisive metric first: steering toward 'conversion' should overwrite the private belief and eliminate snap-back; steering toward 'compliance' should preserve it and increase snap-back. Convincing H4: ≥ 15 pp change in snap-back rate in the predicted direction for each steering polarity, with random-direction < 5 pp, truth-direction not selectively acting, perplexity increase < 10% and MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp and NO-PRESSURE accuracy preserved within 3 pp. Indecision 5–15 pp; < 5 pp means the split is not a steerable component. Experiment 5 (application/predictiveness): a probe-based monitor flags 'merely-compliant' answers that will revert; report precision/recall at an operating point (convincing if precision ≥ 0.7 at recall ≥ 0.5). Experiment 6 (generalization): transfer across pressure types, real vs synthetic, and domains (AUROC retention ≥ 0.65). Thresholds fixed pre-data. Residue/memory controls (to prove the retained signal is a belief, not a token trace): paraphrased and masked-answer re-asks, delayed/noisy intervening context, counterbalanced formats, and a hidden-state subset on trials where the original answer tokens never appear verbatim. Operational gate: a trial counts as 'retained belief' only if the Phase-1 readout predicts the Phase-2 no-pressure answer beyond log-probs, the stated answer, and uncertainty (incremental AUROC >= 0.05). Primary work establishes persistence (H1-H2) on one or two models before localization/steering (H4) is attempted. Application (Experiment 5) reports whether the monitor improves a downstream decision (e.g., withholding a low-confidence 'agreement' in a debate-aggregation task), not only snap-back detection. Power: we report expected conformed-trial counts per model/condition (>= 300 needed for the stated AUROC at 80% power) and scope claims to conditions that meet it.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'retained private belief' probe reading could reflect residual token/context traces of the original answer rather than a genuine maintained belief; matched no-pressure baselines, the synthetic-entity track, comprehension checks, and the snap-back predictiveness test (behavioral confirmation that the retained signal is functional) are designed to distinguish a real private belief from surface residue. Public-private divergence may be rare or absent — a robust result in either direction is informative: high divergence means LLM conformity is skin-deep (reassuring but implies unreliable stated agreement), while genuine conversion means social pressure truly overwrites beliefs (a stronger safety concern), and either finding is publishable. Snap-back could be driven by the neutral re-ask framing rather than a retained belief; we control the PHASE-2 framing, use repeated sampling, and include a within-context variant. Belief probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The compliance vs. conversion components may be entangled or distributed rather than discrete heads; we treat 'steer to eliminate/induce snap-back' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component, and compare to the known compliance subspace. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately stubborn or gullible; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, no-pressure accuracy, and general benchmarks. Instruction-tuned models may conform differently than base models (an interesting comparison but limits universality). Results may not transfer to very large closed models. We avoid anthropomorphic wording throughout: 'private belief' denotes a latent state predictive of the later pressure-removed answer, and all persistence claims are gated on that operational test.

Name: belief_source_tags
Title: Where Did You Hear That? Probing and Steering the Provenance of LLM Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs internally track not only whether they hold a belief about an item's state, but also the epistemic *source* of that belief (pretraining prior vs. in-context assertion vs. tool/retrieval evidence), and this provenance signal is linearly decodable and causally steerable — separately from the truth-value direction. This distinguishes belief-provenance from belief-truth, which prior work conflates. Linear decodability and geometry are validation, not the contribution; the load-bearing novel claim is that a source variable — recovered before answer generation on matched same-proposition/same-truth items that differ only in source — causally gates sycophancy, prior-vs-retrieval conflict resolution, and citation behavior. We add a fourth source regime, unreliable/tool-observation retrieval, to separate provenance from generic in-context text.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs linearly represent belief/truth directions (Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024), belief-state geometry (Transformers represent belief state geometry 2024), agents' beliefs in ToM (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Lookbacks 2025), and world states (Propositional Probes 2024). Critically, the paper 'Language models cannot reliably distinguish belief from knowledge and fact' shows models conflate epistemic categories in their *outputs*. Existing probing work asks 'does the model believe X is true?' but not 'why/from where does it believe X?'. We introduce the orthogonal axis of belief PROVENANCE (prior vs. in-context vs. external evidence) as an internal, decodable, steerable variable. This is not a trivial extension: it reframes the belief-knowledge-fact confusion as a possibly-recoverable internal signal, and offers a mechanistic handle on sycophancy, context-vs-prior conflicts, and RAG faithfulness. Closest prior work and delta, one row each on 'does it isolate source independent of truth?': truth/belief probes (Azaria & Mitchell 2023) read whether a proposition is believed true, not from where (no); sycophancy- and conflict-steering and RAG-faithfulness work act on behavior without isolating an internal source variable (no); belief-state geometry describes truth-state posteriors, not provenance (no); ours decodes source on matched same-proposition/same-truth items and steers it (yes). Probing, activation patching, and contrastive steering are standard tools here; the contribution is the provenance question and the released artifact — a source-controlled dataset with a real-retrieval/tool track, a provenance probe suite, and a sycophancy/RAG-faithfulness steering-and-monitoring benchmark — not the methods. We temper mechanistic language: linear decodability and steerability are evidence for a recoverable provenance representation, not proof of a discrete internal 'tag'.
Abstract: Large language models represent beliefs about the states of items, and prior interpretability work has isolated linear 'truth-value' directions. But a belief has not only a truth-value, it also has a provenance: the model may hold it because of its pretraining prior, because it was asserted in context, or because it came from retrieved/tool evidence. We hypothesize that LLMs internally tag beliefs with their epistemic source, and that this provenance signal is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally steerable. We construct a controlled dataset of item-state claims where we independently vary claim truth and claim source (prior-consistent, prior-contradicting-in-context, and retrieval-attributed), including matched cases where the same proposition arrives from different sources. We train linear probes to decode source and truth on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Pythia), measure their geometric relationship (subspace angles, joint vs. separate decodability), and localize the responsible attention heads via activation patching. We then test causal control: does steering along the provenance direction change downstream behavior such as sycophancy (adopting user-asserted false claims), citation of sources, and answers under prior-vs-context conflict? We evaluate with probe accuracy, subspace overlap, patching effect sizes, and behavioral metrics (sycophancy rate, context-adherence, source-attribution accuracy). If confirmed, provenance-aware probing offers a practical monitor and controller for RAG faithfulness and sycophancy, and shows that the belief/knowledge/fact confusion in outputs may coexist with a recoverable internal provenance signal. So what: if provenance is decodable and steerable, a deployed system can flag prior-vs-retrieval conflicts, downweight ungrounded priors, and monitor citation faithfulness from internal state rather than output heuristics; if it is fundamentally entangled with truth or answer policy, that is itself an actionable negative for RAG monitoring. We release the source-controlled dataset (including a real-retrieval/tool track), the probe suite, and the steering/monitoring benchmark.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — belief provenance is linearly decodable): Tests whether the epistemic source of a belief (pretraining prior vs. in-context assertion vs. retrieval-attributed) is recoverable from activations, separate from truth. Data: built from scratch, 5,000 item-state propositions (2,500 real subject-relation-object facts subsampled from a ~50k-triple Wikidata export; 2,500 novel synthetic entity-attribute facts to neutralize pretraining priors), each rendered in three matched provenance frames (prior-only bare question; a sentence asserting it; the same claim inside a quoted 'document/tool output'), = 15,000 stimuli, split 70/15/15 by proposition so no proposition crosses splits. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, all frozen; only trainable component is an L2 logistic-regression probe on the residual stream at the state token, fit per layer, regularization C chosen on val over {0.01,0.1,1,10}; 5 resampling seeds. Systems compared: 3-way source probe vs. shuffled-label control probe vs. bag-of-words-on-prompt baseline. Decisive metric first: test macro-AUROC of the source probe at its best layer. Convincing: mean AUROC >= 0.80 with shuffled-label control at 0.50 +/- 0.05 on >=3 of 4 models, and >= 0.05 above the bag-of-words baseline. Indecision band: AUROC in [0.60,0.70) is inconclusive (weak, possibly surface-driven structure) and we do not assert H1. Negative: AUROC < 0.60, or not above bag-of-words by 0.05, means provenance is not linearly encoded at the state token.

Experiment 2 (H2 — provenance is largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction): Tests that source is not a re-description of truth. Using the same stimuli crossed with true/false polarity, fit a difference-of-means truth direction and the source probe direction(s) on train. Decisive metric first: source-probe test AUROC after projecting the truth direction out of activations (and, symmetrically, truth AUROC after projecting source out); secondary: principal subspace angle between the truth direction and the source subspace. Convincing: projected-out source AUROC retains >= 90% of its un-projected value and the subspace angle > 60 degrees. Indecision band: retention 70-90% or angle 40-60 degrees means partial entanglement — reported as such, H2 only partially supported. Negative: retention < 70% or angle < 40 degrees means provenance largely coincides with truth and H2 fails; the entanglement geometry is still reported.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the provenance signal is causally steerable and gates behavior): Tests that moving activations along the source direction changes downstream behavior. Build a steering vector by contrastive activation addition (mean in-context-assertion minus mean prior-only activations) at the best layer from Experiment 1. Data: a held-out 1,000-item prior-vs-context conflict subset where context contradicts the pretraining prior, plus 500 user-asserted-false-claim prompts. Systems compared: source-direction steering vs. random-direction steering vs. truth-direction steering, at matched norms (alpha swept so added-vector norm is 2/4/8% of mean residual norm). Decisive metric first: change in sycophancy rate (fraction adopting the user-asserted false claim) between +context and +prior steering; secondary: context-adherence rate under conflict and 'where did you learn this?' attribution accuracy. Convincing: source steering shifts sycophancy by >= 15 absolute points with random-direction steering shifting < 5 points and perplexity on held-out text rising < 10%. Indecision band: a 5-15 point shift is weak causal evidence, reported as suggestive. Negative: < 5 points beyond random, or the effect equals truth-direction steering, means the signal is not a distinct causal provenance handle.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization of the provenance signal): Identifies the heads/layers carrying source. Using activation patching / causal mediation between matched prior-only and in-context runs of the same proposition, patch per-head outputs and measure the restored source-probe logit. Decisive metric first: number of heads whose individual patch recovers >= 50% of the source distinction, and their layer distribution vs. heads known to carry truth/belief. Convincing: a small (<= 20) reproducible head set across seeds mediates source, only partially overlapping truth heads. Indecision band: a diffuse >50-head set is reported as distributed rather than localized. Negative: no head patch exceeds 20% recovery means the signal is not head-localizable.

Experiment 5 (H1,H3 — generalization): Tests transfer beyond the training distribution. Refit nothing; apply the Experiment-1 probe and Experiment-3 steering vector to (a) held-out item domains and (b) naturalistic RAG-style prompts. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC of the frozen probe on the new domain. Convincing: >= 0.70 transfer AUROC and steering retains >= half its in-domain sycophancy effect. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 transfer is limited generality. Negative: <= 0.60 means the signal is distribution-specific.

Experiment 6 (H3 — applied real-retrieval and same-output control): Tests provenance beyond labeled frames and rules out that the probe reads intended output. Data: a 1,000-item RAG subset built with an actual retriever over a fixed Wikipedia snapshot (real retrieved passages, not 'retrieval-attributed' text), plus a same-output control where the final answer string is held fixed while only source varies. Probing timing is fixed a priori: activations are read after the source cue and proposition are in context but before the first answer token, so the probe tests provenance rather than answer planning. Decisive metric first: source-probe AUROC on real retrieved passages and, on the same-output control, AUROC that must stay >= 0.75 (proving the probe is not reading the response). Convincing: >= 0.75 on both. Indecision band: 0.65-0.75 is limited applied generality. Negative: <= 0.65 on real retrieval, or same-output AUROC collapsing to chance, means the signal is a frame/output artifact.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Provenance may be entangled with surface cues (e.g., quotation marks) rather than an abstract epistemic representation; we mitigate with matched-proposition controls and paraphrase/format perturbations. The three-way source distinction may not be cleanly linearly separable, or may be layer/model-specific. Steering could induce off-manifold degradation of fluency (as noted in belief-manifold work); we monitor perplexity and use small steering magnitudes. Truth and source directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of their entanglement (still informative). Synthetic facts may not fully reflect real pretraining priors; we complement with well-known real facts. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. To rule out that the probe merely reads the intended response, we include a same-output control (answer fixed, source varied) and fix probe timing before the answer token. 'Prior' labels are estimated per model by pretesting closed-book answerability so provenance labels are not noisy. We scope conclusions to evidence for a representation rather than a discrete tag.

Name: continued_influence_belief
Title: Retracted but Not Erased: The Continued Influence of Corrected Misinformation in LLM Belief Representations
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM reads a false claim about an item that is later explicitly retracted in the same context, it verbally acknowledges the retraction yet retains an internally-decodable 'stale belief' in the retracted claim that continues to drive its downstream inferences — an LLM analogue of the human Continued Influence Effect (CIE). This internal residual belief is separable from the model's stated belief, predicts CIE-style reasoning errors, and can be causally erased by intervening on the component that carries it.
Related Work: The Continued Influence Effect / belief perseverance is a canonical, heavily-cited human finding: corrected misinformation continues to influence reasoning even after successful retraction (Chan et al. 2017 meta-analysis; Ecker et al. 2022 Nature Rev Psych; constraint-satisfaction models of perseverance, Read & Marcus-Newhall 2001; DIO model 2025). In LLMs, prior work studies (a) knowledge-editing reversibility and 'superficial editing' (Superficial Editing 2025; Believe It or Not 2025), (b) belief shifts under pretraining poisoning (Layer of Truth 2025), (c) intra-memory knowledge conflict localization (Where Knowledge Collides 2026), and (d) in-context knowledge conflict / sycophancy behaviorally. Crucially, to our knowledge no prior work isolate the CIE signature: a *within-context* retraction event after which the model behaviorally acknowledges the correction yet an internally-decodable belief in the *retracted* claim persists and continues to drive inferences. Prior belief-entrenchment work (Martingale Score; confirmation-bias CoT) concerns gradual non-Bayesian drift, not persistence of an explicitly-corrected proposition. We transfer a specific human-cognition phenomenon into LLMs, dissociate stated-vs-internal belief around a discrete correction, and give it a causal mechanistic treatment (locate + intervene), which is new. Delta to own-answer retraction work: here the false claim is EXTERNALLY supplied and explicitly retracted within the context, so any persistence cannot be explained by the model defending a claim it generated itself — a mechanistically distinct case that Experiment 3's own-answer-vs-external-claim contrast tests directly.
Abstract: People keep using misinformation even after they accept a correction — the Continued Influence Effect (CIE), one of the most robust findings in the misinformation literature. As LLMs increasingly ingest, then are corrected on, false claims within a single context (RAG updates, user retractions, multi-turn edits), we ask whether they inherit CIE at the level of their internal beliefs. We hypothesize that after an explicit in-context retraction of a false item-state claim, an LLM (i) verbally acknowledges the correction but (ii) retains a linearly-decodable residual belief in the retracted claim, (iii) this internal residual belief — not the stated belief — predicts continued reliance on the misinformation in downstream inference, and (iv) the residual can be causally erased by intervening on the component that carries it, reducing CIE-style errors. We build a controlled dataset of narratives/knowledge items in which a false claim is introduced and then retracted (with matched no-retraction and never-introduced controls), using both real-fact and synthetic-entity tracks to control priors, plus downstream inference probes whose correct answer depends on discarding the retracted claim. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief probes to read the internal belief in the retracted claim across layers, compute a per-item CIE residual (internal belief post-retraction minus never-introduced baseline), test whether it dissociates from stated belief and predicts downstream reliance (AUROC vs. a log-prob baseline), localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test a contrastive 'retraction-completion' steering intervention that drives the internal belief to baseline. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, CIE residual magnitude, stated-vs-internal dissociation, reliance-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-intervention error reduction, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 5,000 scenarios built from scratch following the classic Continued-Influence paradigm, in two tracks: (a) ~2,500 real-fact narratives adapted from published CIE stimuli (a report asserts a cause, then retracts it); (b) ~2,500 synthetic-entity items ('Zorblax was reported to orbit Kelvath. Correction: this was an error.') with fully stipulated ground truth to remove pretraining priors. Each item appears in three conditions — RETRACTED, NO-RETRACTION, and NEVER-INTRODUCED (baseline) — with retraction strength varied (bare negation vs. explanatory alternative). Each item carries a stated-belief probe, a downstream open-inference probe whose correct answer requires discarding the retracted claim, and a comprehension check that a correction occurred. Items failing comprehension are dropped; ~4,000 remain. 80/20 item split; downstream open answers scored by an LLM-judge with human validation on a 300-item sample (target inter-rater κ ≥ 0.6).

Experiment 1 (H1 — after an accepted retraction the model keeps an internally-decodable residual belief in the retracted claim that is separable from its stated belief). Read the belief probe at the retracted-claim tokens WITHOUT asking the stated-belief question; CIE residual = belief(RETRACTED) − belief(NEVER-INTRODUCED) per item/layer. Systems compared: internal residual vs. the model's stated belief (which should read false) vs. the NO-RETRACTION condition. Decisive metric: mean CIE residual, and the per-item dissociation rate (stated=false while residual > 0). Convincing: residual ≥ 0.10 with CI excluding 0 in ≥ 3 of 4 models AND dissociation rate ≥ 30%, with explanatory-alternative retractions showing a smaller residual than bare negations (mirroring humans). Indecision band: residual < 0.05 or CI includes 0 → no continued influence internally (a valuable negative: LLMs fully erase corrected claims, unlike humans); 0.05–0.10 = suggestive only.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the internal residual predicts continued reliance on the misinformation beyond what the model says). Collect ground-truth downstream reliance from the open-inference probe. Decisive metric: AUROC of the residual predicting per-item reliance, compared against a log-prob-confidence baseline and against the stated-belief read-out. Convincing: residual AUROC ≥ 0.70 and at least +0.05 AUROC over both baselines (incremental signal). Indecision band: AUROC 0.60–0.70 or increment < 0.05 → residual not shown to add reliance-relevant information; ≤ 0.60 = negative.

Experiment 3 (H3 — the residual is carried by an identifiable component and can be causally erased). Localize via activation patching (RETRACTED↔NEVER-INTRODUCED) to the minimal head/layer set that removes the residual; derive a contrastive 'retraction-completion' steering direction. Decisive metric first: post-steering residual and downstream CIE-error rate; baselines: random-direction and truth-direction steering, plus the Setup guardrails. Convincing: subtraction drives residual to ≤ 0.05 and cuts CIE errors by ≥ 50% relative, cleanly on guardrails; adding the direction increases perseverance; random/truth directions cut errors < 10%. Indecision band: 20–50% error reduction or guardrails only in their 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no component/steer erases the residual without breaching guardrails) means CIE is distributed rather than a modular residual. Generalization (supports H1–H3): transfer across real and synthetic tracks and retraction phrasings, with transfer AUROC ≥ 0.70 and error-reduction retained ≥ 50%.

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The residual could reflect surface co-occurrence of the retracted claim's tokens rather than a genuine belief; matched NEVER-INTRODUCED controls, non-introduced distractors, comprehension checks, and paraphrase perturbations mitigate this. CIE may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs fully erase corrected claims — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans). Stated belief and downstream reliance may both fail simply because the model can't parse the retraction; comprehension checks and the RETRACTED-vs-NO-RETRACTION contrast disentangle parsing failure from perseverance. The residual may not be cleanly linear or single-locus; we report layerwise results and treat 'drive belief to baseline / reduce CIE' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Real-fact CIE stimuli may interact with pretraining priors; the synthetic track isolates the in-context mechanism. Downstream-reliance judgments require careful open-ended scoring (LLM-judge plus human validation on a sample). Steering could degrade fluency or over-suppress legitimately retained information; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_entrenchment_probing
Title: Frozen Minds: Probing and Unfreezing Internal Belief Entrenchment During LLM Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: As an LLM generates a multi-step reasoning trace, its internal belief about the answer to an item becomes progressively 'entrenched': the linearly-decodable belief representation stops updating in response to new evidence introduced later in the trace, even when that evidence should rationally shift it. This internal entrenchment is measurable per-step, precedes and predicts behavioral confirmation bias, and can be causally reduced by steering the residual stream to restore belief plasticity, improving truth-seeking on evidence-integration tasks. Step-wise decodability is a validated premise, not the contribution; the novel claims are (a) that internal plasticity decays and freezes at a locatable point in the trace before textual/logit commitment, and (b) that a targeted plasticity intervention selectively restores late-evidence sensitivity and reversal-item accuracy without making the model indiscriminately swayed by any late text.
Related Work: Prior work establishes that transformers linearly represent belief states (Transformers Represent Belief State Geometry, 2024; Constrained Belief Updates, 2025) and that a 'solvability belief' axis is decodable but causally inert for execution (Confidence is Not Competence, 2025). Behaviorally, the Martingale Score (2025) shows LLM reasoning violates Bayesian martingale updating (belief entrenchment) at the output level, and Confirmation Bias in CoT (2025) shows prior beliefs skew reasoning. The Hypocrisy Gap (2026) contrasts a static internal belief with the CoT text. NONE of these track the trajectory of the internal belief representation itself across reasoning steps, characterize *when/where* it freezes relative to evidence arrival, or test a causal intervention to restore plasticity. We reframe entrenchment as an internal, per-step representational dynamics phenomenon and ask whether it is a causally editable failure mode, distinguishing our proposal from behavioral (Martingale) and static-belief (Hypocrisy Gap) approaches. Closest work and delta: the Martingale Score (2025) measures non-Bayesian updating at the output level — we measure the internal belief trajectory and its temporal freezing; Confirmation Bias in CoT (2025) shows priors skew reasoning behaviorally — we localize when/where the internal belief stops updating; belief-state-geometry work (2024) characterizes static geometry — we characterize its dynamics under delayed disconfirming evidence and a causal rescue. Probing, patching, and steering are standard tools; the contributions are the read-time freezing phenomenon and the plasticity intervention. Released artifact: an ordered-evidence 'late-reversal' benchmark with comprehension-matched controls, a per-step plasticity metric, and an entrenchment head map.
Abstract: When a language model reasons step-by-step, its final answer often confirms a hypothesis formed early, even when later steps surface contradicting evidence, a behavior known as confirmation bias or belief entrenchment. Prior studies measure this behaviorally or contrast a single static internal belief against the reasoning text. We instead track the internal belief representation itself as it evolves across reasoning steps. We hypothesize that entrenchment is a representational dynamics phenomenon: an LLM's linearly-decodable belief about an item's answer initially updates with incoming evidence but then 'freezes,' becoming insensitive to later, decision-relevant evidence. We construct controlled evidence-integration tasks in which pieces of evidence pointing toward different answers are revealed in a specified order within the prompt or generated trace, so that the rationally-updated belief has a known ground-truth trajectory. We train linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, and a reasoning-tuned R1-distilled model) and measure, at each step, (i) the probe belief, (ii) its agreement with the rational Bayesian trajectory, and (iii) a per-step plasticity score (belief change per unit of new evidence). We test whether plasticity decays over the trace, whether an early-freezing signature predicts final-answer errors, and whether it correlates with behavioral entrenchment metrics like the Martingale Score. Finally, we identify the layers/heads mediating freezing via activation patching and test a causal 'unfreezing' intervention: injecting a plasticity direction (contrastive activation addition derived from high- vs. low-plasticity steps) to restore late-evidence sensitivity. We evaluate with probe/rational-agreement curves, plasticity decay slopes, entrenchment-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, and post-intervention accuracy and fluency. So what: late-evidence neglect drives costly errors in medical-triage dialogue, multi-hop retrieval, and tool-augmented agents that must revise on new observations; an online plasticity intervention is a cheap engineering fix and the freezing phenomenon is a mechanistic account. We report both scientific (mechanistic explanation) and engineering (inference-time rescue) impact, and release the benchmark, metric, and head map. To keep the contribution crisp we treat decodability, freezing, and prediction (E1-E3) as primary and localization/intervention (E4-E5) as confirmatory.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — an internal belief representation is linearly decodable and updates step-by-step): Tests that a per-step belief about the answer exists. Data: built from scratch, 4,000 ordered-evidence items (multi-clue deduction puzzles, sequential-evidence forecasting, updating-diagnosis vignettes, and synthetic entity-attribute clue tasks) each with a synthetic-set oracle Bayesian belief trajectory; split 70/15/15 by item. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, all frozen; trainable component only a logistic-regression belief probe P(answer=A) on residual activations at each reasoning-step boundary, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: belief probe vs. shuffled-label control. Decisive metric first: probe test AUROC for the current-favored answer at each step. Convincing: mean AUROC >= 0.80 with control at 0.50 +/- 0.05 on >=3 of 4 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 means the belief is only weakly decodable and per-step trajectories are unreliable. Negative: < 0.60 means no decodable step-wise belief and the remaining experiments are not interpretable.

Experiment 2 (H2 — the belief freezes: plasticity decays across the trace): Tests that late, decision-relevant evidence stops moving the belief. Use the 'late-reversal' condition (early evidence favors A, decisive later evidence favors B) vs. a matched 'consistent' condition. Define per-step plasticity = |delta probe-belief| per unit of oracle-expected belief change. Decisive metric first: slope of plasticity vs. step position (reversal condition), and post-reversal rational-agreement = correlation between probe and oracle trajectory. Convincing: significantly negative plasticity slope (bootstrap 95% CI excludes 0) and post-reversal agreement < 0.3 while consistent-condition agreement > 0.6. Indecision band: post-reversal agreement 0.3-0.5 is partial entrenchment. Negative: no slope difference and high post-reversal agreement means beliefs stay plastic (no entrenchment).

Experiment 3 (H3 — early freezing precedes and predicts behavioral confirmation bias): Tests that the internal signature forecasts final-answer errors. Decisive metric first: AUROC using late-step plasticity to predict final-answer error on reversal items, compared against a log-prob confidence baseline and the behavioral Martingale Score computed on the same runs. Convincing: plasticity AUROC >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 or within 0.05 of log-prob is weak added value. Negative: <= 0.60 or no gain over log-prob means the internal signature is not predictive.

Experiment 4 (H2 — localization of the freezing): Finds where stale belief is carried. Activation patching from post-reversal (updated) into pre-reversal (stale) runs; measure heads/layers whose patch restores late-evidence sensitivity in the probe. Decisive metric first: fraction of the entrenchment effect recovered by the top head set. Convincing: a reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse recovery reported as distributed. Negative: no head exceeds 20% recovery.

Experiment 5 (H3 — causal unfreezing restores plasticity): Tests that steering re-opens late-evidence sensitivity. Build a plasticity CAA vector (high- minus low-plasticity step activations) applied during late steps, alpha swept to 2/4/8% residual norm. Systems compared: plasticity steering vs. random-direction steering. Decisive metric first: final-answer accuracy delta on reversal items; secondary: restored post-reversal probe-oracle agreement, and collateral GSM8K/MMLU-subset accuracy and perplexity. Convincing: >= 10-point accuracy gain on reversal items with < 3-point drop on consistent items and < 10% perplexity rise; random steering < 3-point gain. Indecision band: 3-10 point gain is suggestive. Negative: < 3 points beyond random, or the model becomes indiscriminately swayed by any late text (consistent-item accuracy falls > 5 points), means no clean causal plasticity handle.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe and steering vector across task domains and to naturalistic RAG prompts. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC of the probe. Convincing: >= 0.70 and steering retains half its accuracy effect. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 limited. Negative: <= 0.60 distribution-specific.

Experiment 7 (H1,H3 — temporal precedence and applied late-evidence setting): Tests that internal freezing precedes behavioral commitment and holds when decisive evidence arrives via retrieval/tool output. Data: a 1,000-item agentic subset (adapted multi-hop retrieval and tool-correction dialogues) where a decisive document/observation arrives late. Decisive metric first: lead time in steps between internal plasticity collapse and the point at which next-token logits commit to the early answer; secondary: reversal-item accuracy with vs. without the plasticity intervention in the agentic setting. Convincing: internal collapse precedes logit commitment by >= 1 step on a majority of reversal items and the intervention recovers >= 10 points of agentic reversal accuracy. Indecision band: simultaneous collapse/commitment is reported as co-occurring, not precedent. Negative: commitment precedes internal collapse means the internal signal is a readout, not a driver.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Belief 'freezing' may reflect that the model simply cannot parse late evidence rather than an entrenchment failure; the matched consistent/reversal design and evidence-comprehension checks help disentangle these. The internal belief may not be cleanly linearly decodable at every step, or may be distributed across layers, complicating per-step trajectories; we use multi-layer probes and report layerwise results. The plasticity steering direction could degrade fluency or overshoot (making the model unstable/gullible to any late text); we monitor perplexity, use small magnitudes, and evaluate on consistent-condition and general benchmarks. Oracle Bayesian trajectories are only exact on synthetic sets; naturalistic items rely on approximate rational baselines. Reasoning-tuned models may show qualitatively different dynamics than base models, which is itself an interesting comparison but limits universal claims. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. We prioritize E1-E3 plus one of E4/E5 for a single paper rather than claiming phenomenon+localization+intervention at once. Significance uses bootstrap CIs with multiple-comparison correction across layers/heads and preregistered falsification conditions (e.g., high post-reversal agreement falsifies freezing). Probe validity is checked against decoding from step text alone, the previous-step hidden state, and randomized evidence order.

Name: belief_rigidity_ontogeny
Title: Learning to Be Stubborn: The Developmental Emergence of Belief Entrenchment Across Pretraining
Short Hypothesis: As a language model pretrains and a fact's parametric belief strengthens, the model's willingness to OVERRIDE that belief with in-context counter-evidence progressively DECAYS: per-fact, the pretraining checkpoint at which a belief becomes linearly decodable predicts the checkpoint at which that belief becomes context-unrevisable. Belief entrenchment (the failure of RAG-style in-context correction) is thus an emergent ontogenetic property that co-develops with, and is causally tied to, parametric belief consolidation rather than being a fixed trait of the final model. (Throughout, "belief" denotes an internal, probe-decoded belief-state proxy, validated against behavior, not a claim of phenomenal belief.)
Related Work: Pretraining-dynamics work characterizes WHEN factual knowledge is acquired and forgotten (How Do LLMs Acquire Factual Knowledge 2024; How do LMs learn facts 2025 - three-phase plateau; Probing Across Time 2021), that linear representations of relations form at frequency thresholds (On Linear Representations and Pretraining Data Frequency 2025), and that KNOWLEDGE ENTROPY decays over pretraining, impairing new-knowledge integration (Knowledge Entropy Decay 2024). Component-evolution work tracks head/FFN specialization over training (Time Course MechInterp 2025; Crosscoding Through Time 2025). Inference-time work shows final models over-rely on parametric priors and resist in-context correction (context-vs-prior conflict, RAG faithfulness). CRITICALLY, none link the two: no work asks whether, per individual fact, the emergence of a decodable parametric belief CAUSES the loss of in-context revisability (belief entrenchment), nor traces this acquisition-to-rigidity tradeoff across checkpoints, nor tests whether the same mechanism (e.g. knowledge-entropy decay / consolidated recall circuits) that consolidates the belief is what makes it unrevisable. This reframes belief entrenchment as a developmental phenomenon with a per-fact ontogenetic timeline, distinct from acquisition/forgetting dynamics (which ignore in-context override) and from my prior inference-time-only belief proposals. The delta is sharpened to a per-fact CHECKPOINT-COUPLING claim — the checkpoint at which a fact's belief becomes decodable predicts the checkpoint at which its belief becomes context-unrevisable, beyond corpus frequency and item difficulty — not the truism that beliefs strengthen over training. This is distinct from Knowledge-Entropy-Decay (aggregate new-knowledge integration, not per-fact contradictory-context override across checkpoints); to our knowledge no prior RAG-faithfulness/context-conflict work uses checkpoint sweeps. The ontogeny metaphor is de-emphasised in favour of the falsifiable empirical claim. What still counts as a genuinely new claim if the H3 causal result fails: a robust per-fact acquisition->entrenchment coupling beyond frequency/difficulty (H1-H2) is itself novel and useful to pretraining-dynamics researchers, benchmark designers, and RAG evaluators.
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented and correction-based systems assume a model will update its answer when the context contradicts what it knows. Yet models notoriously cling to their parametric priors. We ask a developmental question that prior pretraining-dynamics work has not: does a fact's belief become HARDER to override with in-context counter-evidence as the model learns it more strongly, and are these two timelines causally linked? We hypothesize that (i) for a given fact, there is a checkpoint at which its parametric belief becomes linearly decodable (acquisition) and a later checkpoint at which the model stops revising that belief when the context asserts the opposite (entrenchment); (ii) per-fact acquisition timing predicts entrenchment timing, so belief rigidity co-develops with consolidation rather than being uniform across the final model; and (iii) the consolidation mechanism (a strengthening parametric-recall circuit and declining reliance on context) causally drives the loss of revisability, so that intervening on it restores in-context updatability. Using open pretraining checkpoints (Pythia suite, OLMo-7B) with known training-data frequencies, we build controlled fact sets, present each fact under a matched in-context contradiction, and at each checkpoint measure (a) parametric belief via a linear probe, (b) in-context revision behavior, and (c) an internal 'context-vs-prior reliance' signal. We trace per-fact acquisition and entrenchment curves, test their predictive coupling against frequency and difficulty baselines, localize the consolidating recall component, and causally test whether attenuating it re-opens in-context revisability. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-fact acquisition/entrenchment checkpoints and their correlation, revision-rate trajectories, coupling AUROC vs. baselines, patching/ablation effect sizes, post-intervention revision restoration, and perplexity. Practical consequences are concrete: checkpoint-aware RAG diagnostics, training-time revisability regularisers, and editing methods that target the consolidation circuit. The core value is explaining WHEN models stop honouring corrective evidence (phenomenon impact), separate from the intervention (method impact). If only H1/H2 succeed, benchmark designers and pretraining-dynamics/RAG researchers still benefit; transfer to larger models is argued from the frequency-threshold regularities shared across scales, with generalisation evidence specified rather than assumed.
Experiments:
The hypothesis has three testable parts: H1 — per fact there is a pretraining checkpoint at which its parametric belief becomes linearly decodable (acquisition) and a later checkpoint at which the model stops revising that belief when the context asserts the opposite (entrenchment); H2 — per-fact acquisition timing predicts entrenchment timing, over and above corpus frequency and item difficulty (belief rigidity co-develops with consolidation rather than being uniform); H3 — the consolidation mechanism (a strengthening parametric-recall component and declining context reliance) causally drives the loss of revisability, so attenuating it restores in-context updatability.

Data (built from scratch, over existing fact sets). ~4,000 subject-relation-object facts spanning a wide range of pretraining-corpus frequencies, drawn from CounterFact/T-REx and paired with published OLMo/Pythia term-frequency estimates, plus a matched difficulty control set. We use ~4,000 of the available pool (fewer only where frequency estimates are unavailable). Per fact: a closed-book PARAMETRIC query ("The capital of X is ___"), an IN-CONTEXT CONTRADICTION prompt ("Document: The capital of X is [wrong value]. Question: …") with matched wording, and a NEUTRAL-context control (context restates the true value or is irrelevant); comprehension checks ("quote the context value").

Models (checkpoint sweep — the core resource). Pythia suite at 160M, 1.4B, and 6.9B across its released checkpoints, and OLMo-7B intermediate checkpoints — all frozen at each checkpoint. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen residual-stream activations at the object token, retrained per checkpoint (L2 logistic regression, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, shuffled-label control tasks, mean±sd), corroborated by closed-book log-prob. Steering/ablation via contrastive activation addition and component down-scaling, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — acquisition and entrenchment checkpoints exist). At each checkpoint, per fact, measure (i) PARAMETRIC BELIEF (probe + log-prob), (ii) IN-CONTEXT REVISION (does the model output the contradicted context value?), (iii) a CONTEXT-vs-PRIOR reliance signal (attention-to-context + patching-based attribution). Define the ACQUISITION checkpoint (first crossing a belief-probe criterion) and the ENTRENCHMENT checkpoint (first checkpoint where revision rate drops below a criterion). Decisive metric first: fraction of facts for which both a well-defined acquisition and a later entrenchment checkpoint exist, with entrenchment lagging acquisition. Convincing: ≥60% of facts show acquisition-then-entrenchment ordering with entrenchment ≥ acquisition, in ≥2 of the model families. Indecision band: 40–60% — ordering unclear for many facts. Negative (<40%, or entrenchment routinely precedes acquisition): the two-timeline picture fails — H1 rejected (still informative: rigidity is present from first acquisition or absent).

Experiment 2 (H2 — coupling beyond frequency/difficulty). Decisive metric: per-fact correlation between acquisition and entrenchment checkpoints, and the partial correlation controlling for corpus frequency and difficulty (partial regression). Convincing: raw correlation r ≥ 0.4 AND partial correlation (after removing frequency + difficulty) with CI excluding 0, in ≥2 families; high-frequency facts entrench earlier. Indecision band: partial correlation CI touching 0 while raw r ≥ 0.4 — coupling may be frequency-driven; report as unresolved. Negative (raw r < 0.2): timings are uncoupled — H2 rejected.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal role of the consolidating component). Localize at a mid/late checkpoint via activation patching / attention attribution the parametric-recall component (heads/FFNs) that carries the entrenched belief and suppresses context reliance; track its strength across checkpoints (should rise as entrenchment sets in). Then on late (entrenched) checkpoints attenuate it (ablation / down-scaling, or steering along a context-reliance direction derived from revised-vs-unrevised activations) and test: (a) in-context revision on contradicted facts is restored; (b) specificity — random-component ablation does not restore revision, and neutral-context accuracy is preserved; (c) collateral — a general benchmark subset (1k items) and WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric first: revision-rate recovery on contradicted facts under attenuation, with random-component control. Convincing: ≥15-percentage-point revision recovery, random control <5 pt, neutral-context accuracy preserved (<3 pt drop), <5% perplexity rise, and a monotone component-strength-vs-checkpoint curve. Indecision band: 5–15 pt recovery or a noisy component-strength curve — partial/uncertain. Negative (<5 pt recovery or matched by control): consolidation does not causally drive entrenchment — H3 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.


Robust operationalisation, controls, and design. Acquisition and entrenchment criteria are pre-registered with smoothing and robustness checks and defined via MULTIPLE metrics — closed-book log-prob margins and forced-choice accuracy, not only probe thresholds — so the main claim does not hinge on drifting probes; probe comparability across checkpoints is handled with fixed readout spaces / representational alignment, and a NON-probe metric serves as the primary where possible. We disentangle context-following ability from belief rigidity with supportive-context and irrelevant-context controls plus a per-checkpoint context-copying/comprehension benchmark, and replace attention weights with causal mediation / activation patching / logit decomposition as the reliance metric. Synthetic templated contradictions with unambiguous correct context answers isolate revisability from generation variability. Difficulty is defined independently of frequency (e.g. relation type and answer-set size), not as a vague 'matched set'.

Statistical analysis plan and scope. H2 is fit with a hierarchical model over facts/checkpoints/families (not only per-fact correlations), with bootstrap 95% CIs and Benjamini-Hochberg correction; a power analysis fixes facts-per-frequency-band. To avoid being mechanistically underpowered yet computationally overbroad, the initial scope is ONE Pythia size plus OLMo (one family) first, then expansion. H3 specificity uses neighbouring-component ablations, matched-magnitude random directions, and unrelated-task tests to show the intervention is not merely increasing suggestibility. The PRIMARY endpoint is the Experiment 2 (H2) partial correlation of acquisition and entrenchment checkpoints after removing frequency and difficulty; thresholds are heuristic desiderata. Minimum-viable narrative: a robust behavioural entrenchment curve -> coupling beyond frequency -> one conservative causal intervention.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Entrenchment could simply track corpus frequency rather than a distinct consolidation-to-rigidity mechanism; the frequency-matched difficulty controls and the partial-regression predictiveness test (belief strength beyond frequency) are designed to isolate the belief-consolidation contribution. The acquisition-then-entrenchment ordering may not hold for all facts, or the two timelines may be inseparable (a fact might be revisable and unlearned, or entrenched from first acquisition) - a robust finding either way (coupled vs. decoupled ontogeny) is informative and publishable. In-context revision behavior depends on prompt scaffolding and could reflect instruction-following rather than belief rigidity; comprehension checks, neutral-context controls, and multiple contradiction phrasings mitigate this, though base (non-instruct) checkpoints may under-follow context, which we treat as part of the developmental signal and compare across contradiction strengths. The linear belief probe may not be cleanly decodable or comparable across checkpoints (representations drift); we retrain probes per-checkpoint with control tasks and corroborate with log-prob measures. The recall component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'attenuate to restore revisability' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact unit. Checkpoint availability limits us to Pythia/OLMo (specific data mixes); results may not transfer to other pretraining regimes or to very large closed models. Restoring context-reliance via intervention could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately gullible to any context; we use small magnitudes, random-component baselines, and monitor perplexity, neutral-context accuracy, and general benchmarks.

Name: illusory_truth_internal
Title: Say It Again: In-Context Repetition Inflates LLMs' Internal Belief Confidence Independent of Truth
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human illusory-truth effect, merely repeating a claim within an LLM's context monotonically inflates the model's internally-decoded belief/confidence in that claim as a dose-response of repetition count, independent of (and even against) the claim's factual truth. This repetition-driven inflation is carried by an identifiable internal component (a 'familiarity/fluency' direction or set of heads) that is causally dissociable from the truth-value direction: ablating it restores truth-tracking without removing the model's ability to represent truth.
Related Work: The illusory-truth effect — repetition raising perceived truth and, separately, subjective confidence independent of factual truth — is among the most robust findings in cognitive psychology (Dechene et al.; Fazio et al. 2015; Hassan & Barber 2021 on repetition frequency; Unkelbach 2010 on fluency-as-cue; illusory-certainty 2024 showing repetition inflates confidence orthogonally to truth). In LLMs, repetition has been studied only at TRAINING time: 'Scaling Laws of Learning from Repeated Data' (2022) links repeated pretraining data to induction-head damage and memorization; 'Learning and Unlearning of Fabricated Knowledge' (2024) studies durability of injected facts; 'Layer of Truth' (2025) studies continual-pretraining poisoning shifting late-layer beliefs. The truth-probe literature (Geometry of Truth 2023; Azaria & Mitchell 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024) isolates a linear truth direction; CCPS (2025) probes confidence via representation stability. Critically, to our knowledge to our knowledge, no work asks whether IN-CONTEXT (inference-time) repetition inflates an INTERNALLY-DECODED belief/confidence as a dose-response, orthogonally to truth, and whether that inflation is a locatable, ablatable fluency/familiarity component distinct from the truth direction. We transfer a canonical human-cognition phenomenon into LLM internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment.
Abstract: People judge repeated statements as truer and grow more confident in them, even when the statements are false — the illusory-truth effect, a fluency-driven bias separable from actual discrimination ability. As LLMs increasingly ingest contexts where the same claim recurs (repeated user assertions, echoed retrieval passages, multi-document redundancy), we ask whether they inherit this bias at the level of their internal beliefs. We hypothesize that (i) merely repeating a claim within the context monotonically inflates the model's internally-decoded belief/confidence in it as a dose-response of repetition count, (ii) this inflation is largely independent of the claim's factual truth and can push false claims toward 'believed', (iii) it is mediated by an identifiable internal 'familiarity/fluency' component that is causally dissociable from the well-studied truth-value direction, and (iv) ablating that component restores truth-tracking without destroying the model's representation of truth. We build a controlled dataset of matched true and false item-state claims each embedded in contexts that repeat the claim 0 to N times (with paraphrased-repetition and unrelated-filler controls to separate meaning-level repetition from token/length confounds), including a synthetic-entity track to control pretraining priors. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear belief and confidence probes, measure the repetition dose-response of the internal readout separately for true and false claims, quantify the truth-independent inflation, geometrically relate the repetition-inflation direction to the truth direction, localize responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering/ablating the inflation direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, per-count belief/confidence dose-response slopes, truth-independence of inflation, subspace angle vs. truth, patching effect sizes, post-ablation truth-tracking restoration, and perplexity.
Experiments:
Setup shared by all experiments below. Models: four frozen open-weight base LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B; model weights are never updated (frozen), the only trainable objects are lightweight linear read-out probes and difference-of-means steering vectors. Probes: L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers (or ridge regressors for graded read-outs) fit on residual-stream activations at the named token, one probe per layer, regularization set by 5-fold cross-validation; every probe is trained and evaluated with 5 seeds {0,1,2,3,4} (mean±95% CI reported) and paired with a shuffled-label control task. A probe counts as genuinely reading the target attribute only if held-out AUROC ≥ 0.75 while its control-task AUROC ≤ 0.55; the band 0.55–0.75 (or control AUROC > 0.55) is the indecision zone — that layer/model is reported as 'representation too weak to interpret', not as evidence. Steering vectors are contrastive difference-of-means (activation-addition) directions between the two matched conditions named in each experiment; steering strength is swept over 5 magnitudes and reported as a dose-response. Collateral-damage guardrails for every causal intervention: perplexity on held-out text must rise ≤ 5% and 5-shot MMLU (1k-item subset) must drop ≤ 2 points to count as 'clean'; 5–10% perplexity or 2–4 MMLU points is the indecision band (effect real but not cleanly separable); worse than that fails the guardrail.

Data. 6,000 item-state claims built from scratch, balanced true/false, across geography/science/history/trivia, in two tracks: (a) ~3,000 real facts the models reliably know or disbelieve; (b) ~3,000 synthetic novel-entity claims ('Zorblax orbits Kelvath') with stipulated truth to remove priors. Each claim is embedded in contexts repeating it k ∈ {0,1,2,4,8} times among neutral filler, with four repetition regimes: verbatim, paraphrased (same proposition, new surface form), length-matched-filler-with-single-mention (context-length control), and repeated-unrelated-distractor (generic-repetition control). A behavioral truth-judgment-plus-confidence probe and comprehension checks accompany each item; ~5,000 items pass filtering; 80/20 split with no claim shared across splits.

Experiment 1 (H1 — in-context repetition monotonically inflates the internally-decoded belief/confidence as a dose-response of count). Read the linear belief probe and a representation-stability confidence probe at the final query occurrence, separately for true and false claims, at each k. Decisive metric: slope of internal read-out vs. k. Systems compared: verbatim vs. paraphrased repetition vs. the length-matched and distractor controls. Convincing: positive, monotonic slope significant (CI excluding 0) for BOTH true and false claims in ≥ 3 of 4 models, present under paraphrase (implicating a meaning-level signal) and ABSENT for the distractor/length controls (specificity). Indecision band: slope CI includes 0, or slope present only for true claims (consistent with rational accumulation, not illusory truth) → negative result. 

Experiment 2 (H2 — the inflation is truth-independent and geometrically distinct from the truth direction). Quantify the belief shift attributable to k after conditioning on ground truth; compute the subspace angle between the repetition-inflation direction (high-k minus k=0 difference-of-means) and the linear truth direction, and test whether inflation remains decodable after projecting out truth. Decisive metric: truth-independent inflation magnitude (belief units) and subspace angle. Convincing: truth-independent inflation ≥ 0.10 with the false-claim dose-response still positive, and angle > 60° with inflation still decodable (AUROC ≥ 0.75) after projecting out truth. Indecision band: inflation 0.05–0.10 or angle 45–60° → inflation entangled with truth (characterize, do not claim orthogonality); < 0.05 = negative.

Experiment 3 (H3 — inflation is carried by an identifiable familiarity/fluency component whose ablation restores truth-tracking). Localize via patching high-k→k=0 runs (contrast with copying/induction heads); derive the inflation steering direction. Decisive metric first: behavioral truth-judgment accuracy on repeated-FALSE items after ablation; secondary: internal belief on repeated-false driven back toward k=0, then Setup guardrails; baselines random/truth directions. Convincing: ablation raises repeated-false accuracy by ≥ 15 points and returns internal belief to within 0.05 of k=0, cleanly on guardrails, while random/truth steering do not selectively fix repeated-false items. Indecision band: 5–15 point gain or guardrails only in the 5–10%/2–4-point band. A negative result (no ablatable component restores truth-tracking) means the fluency bias is not modular. Generalization: transfer across domains, real vs. synthetic tracks, and repetition types (transfer AUROC ≥ 0.70).

Statistical analysis (all experiments). Effects are estimated with mixed-effects models carrying random intercepts for item and for model family, so results are pooled across the four models without pseudo-replication; every rate, slope, AUROC, and effect size is reported with a bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 item-level resamples). Multiplicity across layers, heads, and steering magnitudes is controlled with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at q = 0.05. H1 is the pre-registered primary hypothesis; H2 is secondary and the localization/steering hypothesis is confirmatory-exploratory, reported as such unless its pre-stated causal criterion is met.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Repetition-driven belief change might be rational evidence accumulation rather than a fluency bias; the false-claim dose-response (repetition should NOT raise belief in a false claim if the model is rational), the paraphrased-repetition condition, and the repeated-distractor/length-matched controls are designed to dissociate genuine illusory-truth from evidence integration and length/token confounds. The effect may be absent internally (a robust negative result — LLMs resist in-context repetition bias — would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with humans). Belief and confidence probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks and separate the two probes. The inflation and truth directions may be more entangled than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). Localization may yield a distributed rather than discrete component; we treat 'ablate to restore truth-tracking' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Real-fact repetition interacts with pretraining priors; the synthetic track isolates the in-context mechanism. Steering could degrade fluency or blunt legitimate in-context updating; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-repeated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: recognition_truth_leak
Title: It Feels Familiar, So It Must Be True: A Recognition-to-Truth Leak in LLM Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring the human recognition-based truth effect (statements that merely feel recognized are judged truer, an effect that outweighs actual repetition), an LLM's internally-decoded belief in a claim's TRUTH is inflated by its internal FAMILIARITY/RECOGNITION signal for the claim's entity, independent of (and even against) whether the model actually knows the relevant fact. This recognition-to-truth leak is linearly decodable, largely orthogonal to whether the fact is genuinely known, predicts familiarity-driven hallucination, and is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to decouple recognition from truth. (Throughout, "belief" denotes an internal, probe-decoded belief-state proxy, validated against behavior, not a claim of phenomenal belief.)
Related Work: Human research establishes a recognition-based truth effect: statements JUDGED old (recognized) receive higher truth ratings, and this effect exceeds the effect of actual factual repetition (Recognition-based truth effect 2023); prospective feeling-of-knowing (FOK) is dissociable from actual knowledge and can rest on mere cue-familiarity rather than target-accessibility (FOK & partial knowledge 2016; metacognitive domain specificity 2020). In LLM interpretability, sparse-autoencoder 'entity recognition / knowledge-awareness' directions detect whether the model recognizes an entity and causally gate refusal/hallucination (Do I Know This Entity? 2024); 'factual self-awareness' linear features predict correct recall (Factual Self-Awareness 2025); internal states encode the knowledge-RECALL PROCESS, not truthfulness, so associated hallucinations look like facts (LLMs Do NOT Know What They Don't Know 2025); and truth is linearly decodable (Geometry of Truth 2023). CRITICALLY, none ask whether the RECOGNITION/FAMILIARITY signal CONTAMINATES the TRUTH judgment — whether merely recognizing an entity inflates the internally-decoded belief that a claim about it is true, independent of actual knowledge. Prior recognition work links recognition to refusal/hallucination-likelihood, not to a truth-inflation bias; my prior illusory-truth proposal concerns IN-CONTEXT repetition, whereas here the source is PARAMETRIC recognition/familiarity. We transfer the canonical recognition-based truth effect into LLM belief internals with a mechanistic, causal treatment. Novelty stated as claims, each mapped to the closest prior: (1) they show an entity-recognition direction gates refusal/hallucination — we test whether recognition CONTAMINATES the truth judgment (a truth-inflation bias) independent of knowledge; (2) they show internal states encode the recall PROCESS not truthfulness — we test the specific cross-channel leak recognition->truth; (3) illusory-truth work concerns IN-CONTEXT repetition — here the source is PARAMETRIC recognition/familiarity. The primary delta is the truth-inflation bias itself; separate-channels decoding and steering are causal validation, not the novelty. The estimand is a probe-defined truth-belief readout that we additionally validate behaviourally (truth judgment + hallucination), so it is not merely a confidence/recall proxy.
Abstract: People rate statements they merely recognize as truer, even when recognition carries no diagnostic information — a recognition-based truth effect that can outweigh the effect of genuine repetition, and a cousin of the feeling-of-knowing that rests on cue-familiarity rather than real knowledge. LLMs are known to encode an entity-recognition signal (whether they 'know' a subject) and a separate truth signal, and to hallucinate confidently about familiar-but-unknown entities. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: does the model's recognition/familiarity signal leak into and inflate its belief in a claim's truth, independent of whether it actually knows the relevant fact? We hypothesize that (i) an entity-recognition/familiarity channel and a truth channel are separately linearly decodable, (ii) the recognition channel contaminates the truth channel — claims about recognized entities are internally believed truer, holding actual knowledge constant — an internal signature of the recognition-based truth effect, (iii) the leak is graded with familiarity and largest when the model recognizes the entity but lacks the specific fact, predicting familiarity-driven (associated) hallucination, and (iv) the leak is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to decouple recognition from truth. We build a controlled dataset crossing entity FAMILIARITY (recognized/popular vs. unrecognized/rare, plus synthetic entities) with claim VERACITY (true/false) and KNOWLEDGE status (fact actually known vs. not). On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode recognition, truth, and knowledge, measure their geometry, quantify a per-claim recognition-to-truth leak, test its predictiveness for hallucination, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal steering. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, leak magnitude, leak–hallucination AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering decoupling, and perplexity. The phenomenon-level risk is over-believing familiar-entity falsehoods; downstream this supports retrieval gating when recognition is high but knowledge is low, and abstention calibrated on leak magnitude. If confirmed, expect a measurable reduction in associated hallucinations, concentrated in high-familiarity/low-knowledge domains with clear trust/safety relevance; if recognition does not contaminate truth (a negative), that contrasts with the human recognition-based truth effect. We also flag when the leak is a harmful bias versus a reasonable training-frequency heuristic.
Experiments:
