The hypothesis has four testable parts: H1 — an entity-recognition/familiarity channel, a truth channel, and a knowledge channel are separately linearly decodable; H2 — the recognition channel contaminates the truth channel (claims about recognized entities are internally believed truer, holding actual knowledge and veracity constant), and this leak is graded with familiarity and largest in the recognized-but-unknown cell; H3 — the leak predicts familiarity-driven (associated) hallucination; H4 — the leak is carried by an identifiable component that can be steered to decouple recognition from truth.

Data (built from scratch, entities from existing knowledge bases). ~6,000 subject-relation-attribute claims crossing three factors: (A) ENTITY FAMILIARITY — highly-recognized/popular entities, low-familiarity rare real entities, and fully SYNTHETIC novel entities (never seen), with familiarity set by Wikidata/pretraining-frequency proxies; (B) CLAIM VERACITY — true vs false; (C) KNOWLEDGE status — whether the model actually recalls the correct attribute (measured empirically closed-book). We deliberately populate the diagnostic RECOGNIZED-BUT-UNKNOWN cell (familiar entity, fact not reliably recalled) alongside RECOGNIZED-AND-KNOWN and UNRECOGNIZED cells. Claim surface form is matched across familiarity levels (3 paraphrases) to guard against lexical confounds. We use ~6,000 of ~6,000 (cell sizes balanced; fewer only where a model has too few recognized-but-unknown items). Behavioral truth-judgment probe ("Is this true? + confidence"), comprehension checks; 200 items human-validated.

Models. Frozen open-weight Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B. No transformer weights trained; only linear probes on frozen residual-stream/per-head activations (L2 logistic regression per layer, item-disjoint 80/20, 5-fold CV, seeds {0,1,2}, shuffled-label control tasks, mean±sd). Steering via contrastive activation addition, α ∈ {±2,±4,±8} × per-layer std.

Experiment 1 (H1 — three channels decodable). At the entity/attribute tokens (without asking the truth question), train probes for (R) RECOGNITION/FAMILIARITY, (T) TRUTH-VALUE, and (K) KNOWLEDGE, with control tasks. Then compute pairwise subspace angles and test that truth remains decodable after projecting out recognition, and that recognition is distinct from the knowledge direction. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of each of R, T, K vs control-task chance. Convincing: each ≥ 0.75 in ≥3 of 4 models with controls at chance. Indecision band: any channel 0.65–0.75 — weakly decodable. Negative (R or T ≤ 0.65): the required channels are not represented — H1 rejected.

Experiment 2 (H2 — recognition-to-truth leak). Define per-claim leak = shift of the internal truth readout toward "true" as a function of recognition, holding knowledge and veracity constant (recognized-but-unknown vs unrecognized cells, matched FALSE claims). Decisive metric: mean leak on matched-false claims, tested > 0, and largest in the recognized-but-unknown cell; additionally compare the leak's size to a matched in-context-repetition manipulation (test recognition > repetition, mirroring the human effect). Convincing: leak ≥ 0.10 (truth-readout units) with CI excluding 0, peaking in recognized-but-unknown, in ≥3 models. Indecision band: leak 0.03–0.10 — weak. Negative (≤0.03): recognition does not contaminate truth — H2 rejected (a valuable contrast with the human recognition-based truth effect).

Experiment 3 (H3 — leak predicts hallucination). Decisive metric: AUROC of the per-claim leak (read before any query) predicting associated hallucination (confidently asserting a false attribute about a recognized entity), vs a log-prob baseline and the knowledge probe. Convincing: leak AUROC ≥ 0.70 and ≥ 0.05 over both baselines in ≥3 models. Indecision band: 0.60–0.70 or <0.05 over baselines — suggestive. Negative (≤0.60): leak does not predict hallucination — H3 rejected.

Experiment 4 (H4 — localization and causal decoupling). Via activation patching, patch recognized↔unrecognized entity activations to find the minimal component that transports recognition into the truth readout; compare to entity-recognition SAE directions and truth heads. Derive a recognition-to-truth-leak steering direction (controlling for knowledge) and test: (a) subtracting it decouples recognition from truth — lowering unwarranted belief in false claims about recognized entities and reducing associated hallucination; (b) amplifying exaggerates the leak; (c) specificity — random/truth directions do not selectively decouple, genuine-knowledge recall preserved; (d) collateral — MMLU (1k subset), known-fact accuracy, WikiText perplexity (2k lines). Decisive metric first: reduction in associated-hallucination rate under subtractive steering, with controls. Convincing: ≥30% relative hallucination reduction, known-fact accuracy preserved (<2 pt drop), controls <10%, <5% perplexity rise. Indecision band: 10–30% reduction — partial. Negative (<10% or matched by controls): no steerable decoupling component — H4 rejected. All results are planned, not measured.


Rigorous recognised-but-unknown definition, controls, and baselines. 'Unknown' is established with multiple knowledge measurements (greedy + sampled recall, multiple templates, and MCQ verification) to avoid false 'unknown' labels, and entity/fact selection avoids relation-difficulty confounds. Popularity/base-rate controls match entity frequency, relation frequency, and claim prior plausibility, with frequency-mimicking synthetic anchors, so the leak is separated from valid frequency-based inference. We ablate against confidence/log-prob/yes-bias/answerability probes and require the leak to add INCREMENTAL predictive value after conditioning on them. H4 steering specificity uses matched-random, truth-only, and familiarity-only directions with off-target degradation checks across relations/entities.

Statistical analysis plan. Unit of analysis is the claim; we report bootstrap 95% CIs, fit mixed-effects models with random intercepts for entity and relation and a fixed effect for model family, and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction; a power analysis fixes cell sizes to a minimum detectable leak of 0.03 truth-readout units. A single falsifiable PRIMARY hypothesis and endpoint are stated upfront: the Experiment 2 (H2) recognition-to-truth leak on matched-false claims, peaking in the recognised-but-unknown cell; probe-unit thresholds are replaced by standardized effect sizes tied to false-accept/hallucination rate. Minimum viable scope: H1-H3 with the popularity controls and a lighter causal test, rather than full localisation + steering + benchmark preservation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The leak could reflect legitimate inference (claims about popular entities are, on average, more likely to be true in training data) rather than a spurious recognition-to-truth contamination; the FALSE-claim cells (where recognition and truth diverge), the matched RECOGNIZED-BUT-UNKNOWN vs. UNRECOGNIZED comparison at held-constant veracity/knowledge, and the synthetic-entity anchor are designed to isolate genuine leakage from valid frequency-based inference (though full separation is difficult). The recognition and knowledge channels may be hard to separate (recognition often co-occurs with knowledge); the recognized-but-unknown cell and projected-out analyses are built to dissociate them, and even a characterization of entanglement is informative and directly engages the 'recall-process-not-truth' finding. The effect may be absent internally — a robust negative result (recognition does not contaminate the truth channel) would itself be a valuable, publishable finding contrasting with the human recognition-based truth effect. Familiarity estimated from subject popularity is noisy; we use multiple frequency proxies and the synthetic anchor. The truth/recognition probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The leak component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to decouple recognition from truth' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact head. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model distrust all familiar content; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, known-fact accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models.

Name: belief_ripple_internal
Title: Does the Ripple Happen Inside? Probing Whether LLMs Internally Propagate In-Context Belief Updates Before Being Asked
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM reads a new fact stated in context, it internally updates its belief not only about that fact but, silently and before any query, about logically-entailed related facts. This internal 'ripple' is linearly decodable at the entailed-item representation, is graded and selective (some entailments propagate, others don't), and its magnitude at read-time predicts which downstream ripple queries the model will answer correctly. Ripple failures are thus visible internally at ingestion time, not just at output time. Probing, patching, and steering are machinery; the novelty is the read-time internal-propagation question — whether merely reading a fact silently updates a decodable internal state associated with logically-entailed propositions before any query — and its use as a predictive diagnostic. We downscope the causal-amplification claim to a confirmatory follow-on and use 'decodable internal state associated with entailed propositions' rather than asserting a full 'belief' where not validated.
Related Work: Ripple-effect work (RippleEdits 2023; ChainEdit 2025; PropMEND 2025; GradSim 2024; GIE/SIR 2024; KnowledgeSmith 2025; TRACK 2026) studies whether *edited* or in-context knowledge propagates to related facts, but measures propagation only behaviorally (multi-hop QA accuracy) or via gradient/hidden-space edit-side diagnostics; all require *querying* the related fact. 'Believe It or Not' (2025) and 'Do LMs Have Beliefs?' (2021) probe belief depth/consistency of implanted facts but again read beliefs by querying. None ask whether, upon merely *reading* a fact in context (no edit, no query), the model *spontaneously* updates the internal representation of logically-entailed items, whether that update is decodable at read-time, graded/selective per entailment type, and predictive of ripple success. We reframe the ripple as an internal, read-time representational-propagation phenomenon and provide a linear-probe + activation-patching handle on it, distinct from all output-level and edit-side prior work. Contrast claim-by-claim: edit-side ripple work (RippleEdits 2023; 'Why Does New Knowledge Create Messy Ripple Effects' 2024; ChainEdit/PropMEND 2025) measures propagation via multi-hop QA accuracy or gradient/edit-side diagnostics and always requires querying the entailed fact; in-context belief-probing work reads beliefs by querying. To our knowledge no prior work measures hidden-state changes at the entailed item after reading but before querying — we state this cautiously as a gap rather than an absolute. The single reusable artifact is a read-time internal-ripple diagnostic plus a counterfactual-matched entailment benchmark.
Abstract: Telling a language model 'Jack is Johnny's son' should, if the model reasons coherently, make it also believe 'Jack is Lily-Rose's sibling.' Prior work shows this ripple often fails, but always measures it by *asking* the related question. We ask a sharper, mechanistic question: when the model merely *reads* a new fact in context, does it silently update its internal belief about logically-entailed facts, before any query? We hypothesize that (i) such internal ripple updates are linearly decodable from residual-stream activations at the entailed item's representation, (ii) they are graded and selective across entailment types (e.g., symmetric relations, inverse relations, transitive/multi-hop, type-inheritance), and (iii) the read-time magnitude of the internal update predicts whether the model will answer the corresponding ripple query correctly. We construct controlled synthetic entity-relation graphs with novel entities (to bypass pretraining priors) plus a real-fact track. For each injected base fact, we enumerate entailed facts of known types and measure the internal belief about each entailed fact both before and after the base fact appears in context. We train linear belief probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B), quantify per-entailment-type internal ripple magnitude, test whether it predicts downstream ripple-QA accuracy (AUROC) beyond a log-prob baseline, and localize the heads that carry propagation via activation patching. Finally, we test causal amplification: steering along a 'propagation' direction (contrastive activation addition from strong- vs. weak-ripple cases) to see if it increases both internal ripple magnitude and ripple-QA accuracy. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, internal-ripple magnitude by entailment type, ripple-success prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering accuracy delta, perplexity. So what: a read-time diagnostic would let editing pipelines, context-management, and reliability evaluations predict which entailments will (silently) fail before spending multi-hop QA — improving on output-only ripple tests. The clearest impact is research tooling and scientific understanding rather than broad societal reach, and the real-world bridge is user-provided corrections, retrieval updates, and agent memory in deployed systems. We center the paper on one crisp contribution — read-time internal ripple as a predictive diagnostic with exhaustive controls — and treat localization/amplification as exploratory.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — reading a fact silently updates a decodable belief about entailed items at read-time): Data: built from scratch, 5,000 synthetic entity-relation graphs with novel entities; each BASE fact has enumerated ENTAILED facts by type (symmetric, inverse-relation, transitive/multi-hop, type-inheritance) plus NON-entailed distractors, and a matched BASE-absent control; a real-fact track adapted from RippleEdits (~1,000 items subsampled from its published set for external validity); split 70/15/15 by graph. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Pythia-2.8B, frozen; trainable only a logistic-regression belief probe P(entailed fact holds) at the entailed-item tokens, per layer; 5 seeds. The belief is read WITHOUT ever asking the entailed question. Systems compared: probe vs. shuffled-label control. Decisive metric first: internal-ripple magnitude = probe belief(BASE-present) minus probe belief(BASE-absent) at the entailed item, tested > 0. Convincing: mean ripple magnitude significantly > 0 (bootstrap CI excludes 0) for genuine entailments with probe base AUROC >= 0.75. Indecision band: CI touching 0 or AUROC 0.60-0.70 is weak — reported as no reliable read-time ripple. Negative: ripple magnitude ~ 0 is an informative negative (no spontaneous propagation), reframing ripple failures.

Experiment 2 (H1 — the ripple is graded and selective across entailment types): Decisive metric first: per-type ripple magnitude for symmetric/inverse/transitive/inheritance vs. near-zero for non-entailed distractors. Convincing: genuine-entailment ripple exceeds distractor ripple by >= 0.2 probability (bootstrap CI excludes 0) and types rank-order sensibly. Indecision band: entailment-minus-distractor gap 0.05-0.2 is weak selectivity. Negative: gap <= 0.05 means the signal is non-selective (surface co-occurrence), refuting selectivity.

Experiment 3 (H3 — read-time ripple magnitude predicts downstream ripple-QA success): Query each entailed fact to get ground-truth ripple success/failure. Decisive metric first: AUROC using read-time ripple magnitude to predict per-item ripple-QA success, vs. a log-prob baseline and a GradSim-style edit-side indicator adapted to in-context. Convincing: >= 0.70 and >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60 or no gain over log-prob.

Experiment 4 (H1 — localization): Activation patching from BASE-present into BASE-absent runs to find heads/layers carrying propagation; test whether distinct heads mediate different entailment types. Decisive metric first: fraction of ripple recovered by top heads per type. Convincing: reproducible head sets recover >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — causal amplification): Build a propagation CAA vector (strong- minus weak-ripple base-present activations); inject during reading, alpha 2/4/8% residual norm. Systems compared: propagation steering vs. random-direction. Decisive metric first: increase in ripple-QA accuracy; secondary: internal ripple magnitude increase, distractor specificity (distractors must NOT rise), MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 10-point ripple-QA gain with distractor magnitude rising < 0.05 and perplexity rise < 10%; random < 3 points. Indecision band: 3-10 points suggestive. Negative: < 3 beyond random or distractors spuriously updated.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probe/steering across entailment types, synthetic-to-real, and graph depths (1-hop vs. multi-hop). Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and amplification retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 7 (H1,H3 — logical-selectivity and confound controls): Rules out surface co-occurrence and prior answerability as explanations. Data: counterfactual entity-relation graphs matched on entity co-occurrence statistics, with each genuine entailed fact paired to an equally-plausible non-entailed alternative sharing identical entities; template and entailment-composition folds are held out (not just graphs); base-fact memorization and prior answerability are measured per model. Decisive metric first: entailed-minus-matched-alternative ripple magnitude (identical entities, differing only in logical entailment) and, for prediction, incremental AUROC of read-time ripple over hidden-state norms, final-token log-prob, and lexical baselines after partialling out base-fact salience. Convincing: entailed exceeds matched-alternative ripple (bootstrap CI excludes 0) and read-time ripple adds >= 0.05 AUROC over all baselines. Indecision band: gap 0.02-0.05 AUROC is weak incremental value. Negative: no entailed-vs-alternative gap, or no gain over hidden-state norms, means the signal is co-occurrence or salience.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Read-time internal ripple may be weak or absent (models may only compute entailments when queried), in which case a robust *negative* result is still highly informative for the ripple/editing literature and reframes ripple failures as a lack of spontaneous propagation. The entailed-item probe signal could reflect surface co-occurrence of tokens rather than a genuine belief update; matched BASE-absent controls, non-entailed distractors, and paraphrase perturbations mitigate this. Multi-hop entailments may not have a single clean probe target; we anchor probes at well-defined key tokens and report per-type results. Ripple magnitude and ripple-QA success could both be driven by a common confound (fact salience); we control salience and use partial-correlation analyses. Steering could degrade fluency or spuriously propagate to distractors; we monitor perplexity, specificity on distractors, and general benchmarks, and use small magnitudes with random-direction baselines. Synthetic novel entities may be represented differently from real knowledge; the real-fact track provides a check. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. We tighten 'belief' language to 'decodable internal state associated with entailed propositions' unless strongly validated. Probe targets are anchored at defined key tokens with token-position randomization, paraphrase templates, and swapped near-neighbor distractors to prevent superficial success; train/test splits hold out entire entailment templates and relation compositions, not just graphs. The real-fact track handles conflicts with pretrained knowledge, ambiguity, and contamination explicitly. E4/E5 are exploratory unless pilot evidence supports distinct-head localization and amplification.

Name: essentialist_belief_mutability
Title: Essence or Accident? An Internal Mutability Flag That Gates How Readily LLMs Revise Their Beliefs
Short Hypothesis: Mirroring psychological essentialism, LLMs internally tag a belief about an item's property as either ESSENTIAL/IMMUTABLE (a defining, kind-constituting property that resists change, e.g. 'a tiger is a mammal') or ACCIDENTAL/MUTABLE (a contingent, revisable property, e.g. 'this tiger lives in a zoo'). This mutability flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates the model's revision plasticity: when contradicted in context, beliefs internally tagged immutable resist updating far more than mutable ones, at matched evidence strength, and steering along a single mutability direction reverses this resistance.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs reproduce human essentialist categorization, prioritizing teleological/'what-it-is-for' and constitutive properties over appearance ('You are what you're for', 2023), and human cognitive science establishes essentialism, mutability, and kind-vs-accident distinctions (Psychological Essentialism 2021; Functional Origins of Essentialism 2001; Fact Mutability in Counterfactuals 2007; Generics Designate Kinds 2019). On the LLM-internal side: 'In Praise of Stubbornness' (2025) shows contradictory factual updates cause catastrophic interference and are detectable from features but does NOT distinguish essential vs. accidental facts or link resistance to an internal mutability representation; 'Believe It or Not' (2025) measures belief depth of implanted facts (finding plausibility-dependent brittleness) but not a mutability/essence tag; 'Layer of Truth' (2025) localizes poisoning-induced belief flips to late layers; knowledge-editing work documents conflict/distortion side effects. Truth-probe work isolates a linear truth-value direction (Geometry of Truth 2023; Truth-value judgment 2024). CRITICALLY, none isolate an internal essential-vs-accidental (immutability) representation as a decodable variable orthogonal to truth, nor test whether it causally gates in-context belief revision. We transfer psychological essentialism into LLM belief internals and give it a mechanistic, causal treatment, distinct from all prior behavioral-only essentialism work and from my earlier epistemic-tag proposals (provenance, currency, contestedness, endorsement). Explicit novelty claims: N1 (finding) an essential-vs-accidental MUTABILITY tag is linearly decodable from residual activations; N2 (geometry) it is largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction; N3 (mechanism) it causally gates in-context revision plasticity; N4 (setting) a synthetic novel-kind track stipulates property status in-context, isolating mutability from pretraining confidence. Delta against the closest baselines, one line each: confidence/plausibility probes ('In Praise of Stubbornness' 2025; 'Believe It or Not' 2025) predict brittleness from how strongly a fact is held, not from an essence/accident tag; the truth-direction probe (Geometry of Truth 2023) reads is-it-true, not is-it-revisable; contradiction-resistance measures score updating without attributing it to a decodable mutability axis. None can produce the predicted essential>accidental resistance gap AT MATCHED confidence and truth, which is what N1-N4 jointly require.
Abstract: Humans treat some facts as essential to what a thing is (a tiger is a mammal; water is H2O) and others as accidental and freely revisable (this tiger is in a zoo; this water is warm) - psychological essentialism, one of the most robust findings in cognitive science. As LLMs increasingly ingest, are corrected on, and edit factual claims, a consequential question arises: does a model internally distinguish essential from accidental properties, and does that distinction govern how readily it revises a belief? We hypothesize that LLMs maintain an internal 'mutability' flag that tags a belief as essential/immutable vs. accidental/mutable, that this flag is (i) linearly decodable from residual-stream activations, (ii) largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction, and (iii) causally gates revision plasticity: when the same proposition is contradicted in context with matched evidence strength, beliefs tagged immutable resist updating far more than those tagged mutable, and steering a single mutability direction reverses this asymmetry. We build a controlled dataset of item-property claims labeled essential vs. accidental (with a synthetic-entity track defining novel kinds and stipulating property status to control pretraining priors), each paired with a matched in-context contradiction. On frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) we train linear probes to decode mutability vs. truth, measure their geometry, quantify per-item revision plasticity under contradiction, test whether internal mutability predicts revision resistance beyond surface features, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and test causal control by steering the mutability direction. Metrics: probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, projected-out decodability, revision-plasticity gap, resistance-prediction AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-steering plasticity restoration, and perplexity. The stakes are practical: knowledge-editing, RAG-based correction, and continual knowledge maintenance all assume beliefs are revisable, so a mutability tag that silently blocks correction of 'essential' facts is a concrete failure mode; a mutability readout could route such facts to stronger evidence or heavier editing. If the effect reduces entirely to confidence/plausibility, that too is an informative, publishable constraint on the essentialism-in-LLMs literature.
Experiments: Common setup (shared across all experiments, stated once so no experiment depends on an external pointer): Models are four frozen open-weight LLMs — Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B-v0.3 (base checkpoints; instruct variants added only for the behavioral revision runs). No model weights are trained; the only trainable objects are linear probes (L2-regularized logistic regression, C swept over {0.01,0.1,1,10} by 5-fold CV). All activations are the residual stream at the property/item token, every layer, plus per-head outputs for localization. Three seeds {0,1,2} control probe train/test splits and steering runs; splits are BY ITEM (no item in both train and test) to prevent leakage. Dataset (built from scratch): ~6k item-property claims; two tracks — REAL (biology/chemistry/artifacts/social kinds, properties models reliably know) and SYNTHETIC novel-kind (invented kinds with property status stipulated in-context, wording matched between essential and accidental) — crossed with TRUE/FALSE polarity and paired with a matched in-context contradiction of controlled strength; we generate 6k and use all 6k (≈1.5k per model for probe fitting, the rest held out), reporting per-track. Essential/accidental labels human-validated on a 300-item sample (target Cohen's kappa ≥ 0.7; if 0.5–0.7 we drop borderline items, if < 0.5 the label scheme is revised before any probing). Experiment 1 (H1 — mutability flag is linearly decodable): Fit a MUTABILITY probe (essential/immutable vs accidental/mutable) per layer/model on frozen activations; also fit a TRUTH-VALUE probe (true vs false) for later use. Decisive metric first: held-out test AUROC of the mutability probe at its best layer, against a shuffled-label control task expected at 0.50±0.05. Convincing: AUROC ≥ 0.75 on both tracks. Indecision band 0.55–0.65 (above chance but weak) → H1 judged not established, flag only partially linearly available; AUROC ≤ 0.55 (overlapping control) refutes linear decodability. A negative result means the behavioral essentialism reported for LLMs is not backed by a decodable internal mutability tag. Experiment 2 (H2 — mutability is largely orthogonal to the truth-value direction): Compute the principal angle theta between the mutability and truth probe weight directions, and re-test mutability decodability after projecting out the truth direction (and vice versa). Decisive metric first: theta, with the projected-out AUROC drop as corroboration. Convincing orthogonality: theta ≥ 60 degrees AND projected-out AUROC drop < 0.05. Indecision band theta 30–60 degrees → report as partial entanglement, H2 downgraded to 'partially separable'; theta < 30 degrees means the two are the same axis (H2 refuted, still an informative characterization). Experiment 3 (H3 — the flag causally gates revision plasticity): (a) Behavioral+internal plasticity: present a true claim, then the matched contradiction at matched strength; internal plasticity = change in the truth-probe readout before vs after; behavioral revision = stated post-contradiction answer flip. Decisive metric first: the essential-minus-accidental gap in revision resistance (resistance = 1 - plasticity) at matched contradiction strength. Convincing: essential items resist at least 20 percentage points more than accidental items on BOTH internal and behavioral measures, versus a mutability-independent null (gap 0). Indecision band 5–20 pp → gating present but weak; < 5 pp → no essentialism-driven gating (H3 refuted). (b) Causal steering: derive a contrastive mutability direction (essential vs accidental activations, truth held constant); steer essential items toward 'mutable' and accidental toward 'immutable'. Decisive metric first: change in in-context revision rate in the predicted direction. Convincing: ≥ 15 pp shift with a random-direction baseline < 5 pp, truth-direction baseline not selectively moving plasticity, perplexity increase < 10% and MMLU-subset drop < 3 pp; indecision 5–15 pp; < 5 pp (or collateral damage above the guards) means steering does not establish causality. Experiment 4 (localization, supports H3): activation patching of essential<->accidental activations at the contradiction point to find the minimal head/layer set that increases/decreases plasticity, reported as logit-difference effect sizes; compared to truth/belief heads. Experiment 5 (predictiveness, supports H1/H3): does the pre-contradiction mutability readout predict per-item revision resistance (AUROC) beyond a log-prob confidence baseline and a bag-of-words lexical baseline (target improvement ≥ 0.05 AUROC; < 0.02 means the internal flag adds nothing over surface cues). Experiment 6 (generalization): probe/steering transfer across domains, real vs synthetic tracks, and contradiction strengths, reporting AUROC retention (convincing if ≥ 0.65 cross-domain). All thresholds and bands above are fixed before data collection. Primary hypotheses are H1-H3 (Experiments 1-3); Experiments 4-6 are secondary/localization and Experiment 7 is an applied demonstration. Confound suite (run before any causal claim): regress the mutability probe against per-item confidence (log-prob), token frequency, lexical category, generic-vs-specific sentence form, and subject/object type, and report incremental decodability after residualization (convincing if AUROC drop < 0.05; if the residualized AUROC falls into 0.50-0.55 the tag is a surface artifact). Experiment 7 (application — mutability readout gates correction success): on the REAL track, apply RAG-style in-context correction and a lightweight weight edit (ROME/MEMIT-style single-fact edit) to items pre-scored high vs low mutability; decisive metric first: correction/edit success-rate gap between low-mutability (predicted revisable) and high-mutability (predicted resistant) items. Convincing: >= 15 pp gap that the mutability readout predicts beyond a confidence baseline by >= 0.05 AUROC; indecision 5-15 pp; < 5 pp means the readout has no operational value. Power: with ~1.5k probe-fit items/model and three seeds, a 0.05 AUROC difference is detectable at 80% power (alpha 0.05); we report per-seed variance and cross-model CIs since thresholds are fixed pre-data.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Revision resistance for essential items could reflect that essential facts are simply held with higher pretraining confidence rather than a distinct mutability representation; the synthetic novel-kind track (where essential/accidental status is stipulated in-context rather than reflecting pretraining strength) and matched contradiction strength are designed to dissociate mutability from raw confidence, and the resistance-prediction test conditions on a confidence baseline. The mutability flag may be entangled with surface cues (words like 'by definition', 'is a kind of' vs. 'currently', 'this particular'); we mitigate with diverse framings, paraphrase perturbations, comprehension checks, and the synthetic track where cues are balanced. Mutability and truth directions may be less orthogonal than hypothesized, in which case the finding characterizes their entanglement (still informative). The essential/accidental label is partly graded/subjective; we human-validate and treat borderline items separately. The effect may be absent internally - a robust negative result (LLMs' behavioral essentialism is not backed by an internal mutability representation gating revision) is itself a valuable, publishable finding constraining the essentialism-in-LLMs literature. Probes may not be cleanly linear at every layer; we report layerwise results with control tasks. The gating component may be distributed rather than a discrete head; we treat 'steer to restore/reverse plasticity' as the causal test rather than pinning an exact component. Steering could degrade fluency or make the model indiscriminately revise (or entrench) all beliefs; we use small magnitudes, random/truth-direction baselines, and monitor perplexity, non-manipulated accuracy, and general benchmarks. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. We temper 'internal flag' language: unless the mutability representation is shown robust to the confound suite AND causally specific under steering, we report it as a decodable-but-possibly-distributed mutability signal rather than a discrete flag. Sample size is justified above; effect estimates are reported with cross-seed/cross-model CIs.

Name: persona_belief_contamination
Title: Whose Belief Is It? Separating a Persona's False Beliefs from the Model's Own Inside LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When an LLM role-plays a persona that holds a factually false belief the model itself does not endorse (e.g., a flat-earther, a 19th-century physician), the model maintains a persona-belief representation that is partially distinct from its own-belief representation, but the two are entangled such that adopting the persona *contaminates* the model's own internal belief. We hypothesize both beliefs are simultaneously and linearly decodable, that the degree of own-belief contamination is measurable and predicts factual errors after role-play, and that a 'belief-ownership' direction can be steered to insulate the model's own belief from the persona's. The centerpiece is contamination, not simultaneous decoding: adopting a persona that holds a real-world-false belief shifts the model's OWN internal factual belief, this shift predicts own-voice factual leakage after role-play, and a belief-ownership direction can insulate the own-belief while preserving faithful role-play. Contamination is defined and tested apart from mere instruction-following, answer-format persistence, and activation of a generic persona/assistant axis.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs linearly represent self/other beliefs for Theory-of-Mind (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds 2024) and can steer ToM performance, but the 'self' and 'other' beliefs there are ordinary beliefs either agent could hold about a story world, not cases where the persona holds a belief the model *knows to be factually false about the real world*. Persona work (Assistant Axis 2026; Persona Selection Model 2026) shows a persona/Assistant direction governs behavior and 'persona drift', and self-recognition work isolates a 'self' vector, but neither tracks whether adopting a false-believing persona corrupts the model's own factual belief representation. Neuroscience (Thornton & Mitchell 2019; agent-specific learning signals 2018) finds humans represent their own states more distinctly than others'. We combine these: we introduce a controlled 'persona-vs-self false-belief' paradigm and treat contamination of the model's own belief by a persona as a measurable, localizable, and steerable phenomenon distinct from ToM belief decoding. Unlike prior descriptive persona-drift work, we operationalize contamination at the level of the model's *own factual belief representation* and provide a causal insulation intervention. Delta against the two closest baselines: ToM self/other decoding (Beliefs of Self and Others 2024) concerns beliefs either agent could hold in a story — it would not flag that the 'other' belief is false about the real world, nor predict own-voice leakage; persona-drift/assistant-axis work (2026) tracks behavioral drift along a persona direction — it would attribute our effect to generic persona activation, which we rule out by controlling for assistant-axis magnitude and by a no-persona matched-false-statement control. The novelty is the false-real-world-belief setting plus own-voice leakage prediction and causal insulation, not linear probing. Released artifact: a persona-vs-self false-belief benchmark, a contamination metric, and an insulation steering method.
Abstract: Large language models routinely role-play personas, and users increasingly ask them to speak 'as' a flat-earther, a medieval doctor, or a user who believes a false premise. This raises a mechanistic question with direct safety relevance: when the model adopts a persona that holds a belief the model itself does not endorse, does it keep a clean separation between the persona's belief and its own, or does the persona's false belief contaminate the model's own internal representation? Prior Theory-of-Mind interpretability work decodes self/other beliefs, but only for beliefs either agent could hold in a story; prior persona work characterizes 'persona drift' behaviorally. We study the intersection: personas whose factual beliefs conflict with the model's own knowledge. We build a controlled dataset of real-world item-state facts paired with personas that (dis)believe them, and elicit the model to answer as the persona and then, in a matched clean context, answer in its own voice. We train linear probes on frozen open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B) to simultaneously decode (i) the persona's belief and (ii) the model's own belief, measure their geometric relationship, and quantify a 'contamination' score: the degree to which the model's own-belief representation shifts toward a false persona belief. We test whether contamination predicts post-role-play factual errors, localize the responsible heads via activation patching, and derive a 'belief-ownership' steering direction (contrastive activation addition from own-voice vs. persona-voice activations) to test whether we can insulate the model's own belief while preserving faithful role-play. Metrics: joint probe accuracy/AUROC, subspace angle, contamination score, contamination-error AUROC, patching effect sizes, post-role-play factual accuracy, role-play faithfulness, and perplexity. So what: post-role-play own-voice factual leakage is a concrete deployment risk in customer-support role-play, educational debate, and jailbreak personas; if contamination exists, practitioners should benchmark and steer against it or avoid certain persona patterns, and if it does not, current persona use is safer than feared. We estimate the effect size in realistic multi-turn chat, include at least one instruction-tuned/API model for behavioral validation of external relevance, and release the benchmark, metric, and insulation method.
Experiments:
Experiment 1 (H1 — persona-belief and model-own-belief are simultaneously linearly decodable): Data: built from scratch, 5,000 real-world facts the target models reliably know (verified by >= 90% correct own-voice answering), each with matched OWN, PERSONA-CONCORDANT, and PERSONA-DISCORDANT (false-believing persona) contexts, plus comprehension checks; split 70/15/15 by fact. Model: Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, frozen; trainable component only two logistic-regression probes (persona-belief, own-belief) on residual activations at the state token, per layer; 5 seeds. Systems compared: each probe vs. shuffled-label control. Decisive metric first: test AUROC of each probe at best layer. Convincing: both >= 0.80, controls 0.50 +/- 0.05, on >=2 of 3 models. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70 for either probe is weak. Negative: own-belief probe < 0.60 means own-belief is not separately readable and contamination cannot be measured.

Experiment 2 (H1 — own-belief is represented more distinctly than persona-belief; the two are partially distinct but entangled): Decisive metric first: subspace angle between own-belief and persona-belief directions, plus own-vs-persona probe-margin difference; secondary: projected-out decodability. Convincing: angle in (20,70) degrees (partial distinctness) and own-belief margin significantly larger than persona-belief (paired test, p<0.05). Indecision band: angle < 20 degrees (near-collinear) or > 80 degrees (fully separate) each falsify the 'partially distinct but entangled' claim in opposite directions and are reported as such. Negative for the distinctness sub-claim: no margin difference.

Experiment 3 (H2 — adopting a discordant persona contaminates own-belief, and contamination predicts errors): Decisive metric first: contamination score = shift of the own-belief probe toward the false persona value in the DISCORDANT vs. OWN condition; secondary: AUROC using contamination to predict errors on the step-out-of-character own-voice leakage probe, vs. a log-prob baseline. Convincing: mean contamination significantly > 0 (bootstrap CI excludes 0) and contamination-error AUROC >= 0.70, >= 0.05 above log-prob. Indecision band: contamination CI includes 0, or AUROC 0.60-0.70, is weak. Negative: contamination ~ 0 and AUROC <= 0.60 means personas do not corrupt own-belief.

Experiment 4 (H2 — localization): Activation patching to find heads mediating contamination; compare to persona/Assistant-axis and self-recognition directions from prior work. Decisive metric first: fraction of contamination recovered by top heads. Convincing: reproducible <= 20-head set recovers >= 50%. Indecision band: diffuse = distributed. Negative: no head > 20%.

Experiment 5 (H3 — a belief-ownership direction insulates own-belief without breaking role-play): Build an ownership CAA vector (own-voice minus persona-voice activations); during discordant role-play steer toward 'own' (alpha 2/4/8% residual norm). Systems compared: ownership steering vs. random vs. persona-axis steering. Decisive metric first: reduction in own-voice contamination/error; secondary: role-play faithfulness rate (must stay >= 90% of unsteered), MMLU-subset, perplexity. Convincing: >= 10-point error reduction with faithfulness preserved and perplexity rise < 10%; random < 3 points. Indecision band: 3-10 points suggestive. Negative: < 3 points beyond random, or faithfulness collapses, means no clean insulation handle.

Experiment 6 (H1,H3 — generalization): Apply frozen probes/steering across fact domains, persona types, jailbreak personas, and multi-turn role-play. Decisive metric first: transfer AUROC and error-reduction retention. Convincing: >= 0.70 and half the effect retained. Indecision band: 0.60-0.70. Negative: <= 0.60.

Experiment 7 (H2 — discourse-carryover controls and external validation): Separates genuine own-belief contamination from instruction-following/carryover and checks larger models. Data: the discordant items re-run with a hard context reset, paraphrased and delayed own-voice probes, irrelevant intervening turns, and a no-persona control that states the same false content without a persona; plus a behavioral-only replication on one instruction-tuned/API model. Decisive metric first: own-voice error rate in the discordant condition minus the no-persona matched-false control, after context reset and delay; secondary: assistant-axis magnitude as a covariate, and the API-model behavioral leakage rate. Convincing: contamination survives context reset/delay and exceeds the no-persona control (bootstrap CI excludes 0) and is not explained by assistant-axis magnitude. Indecision band: effect present only without reset is reported as carryover, not contamination. Negative: no excess over the no-persona control means the effect is instruction-following.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Contamination could reflect the model simply obeying the discordant instruction rather than a corrupted internal own-belief; the matched OWN/discordant design, the explicit step-out-of-character leakage probe, and comprehension checks help disentangle instruction-following from genuine belief contamination. Persona-belief and own-belief may not be cleanly linearly separable or may be layer/model-specific; we report layerwise results with control tasks and use joint probes. The two belief directions may be more entangled than hypothesized, in which case the finding becomes a characterization of that entanglement (still informative and safety-relevant). Belief-ownership steering could degrade fluency or break faithful role-play (making the model refuse to stay in character); we monitor perplexity, role-play faithfulness, use small magnitudes, and separate 'reduce contamination' from 'break persona'. Personas whose beliefs are genuinely near the model's uncertainty (contested facts) confound the contamination signal; we restrict the core analysis to facts the model reliably knows. Results may not transfer to very large closed models. 'Own belief' is validated with multiple probes/tasks showing convergence beyond immediate response policy, and probes use delexicalized/paraphrased prompts with persona-template splits so they cannot exploit surface form. Localization includes random-head and known-assistant/persona-direction controls to show selected heads are belief-specific rather than generic role-play heads. Steering faithfulness is judged with semantic role-play rubrics, not only perplexity. The core analysis is restricted to facts the model reliably knows so contested-fact uncertainty does not confound contamination.
